titre: “Writing history with lightning”: the source of Wilson's phrase is missing
accroche: Wilson is quoted at a screening of *The Birth of a Nation*: “like writing history with lightning.” Benbow cannot find it in any of the newspapers he consults.
contenu_vulgarise:
On February 18, 1915, in the East Room of the White House, President Woodrow Wilson, his cabinet, his general staff and their families attend a screening of *The Birth of a Nation*. It is the writer Thomas Dixon, who knew Wilson at university, who requested the session. D. W. Griffith made the trip from the West Coast to arrange the details. The next day, the film is shown to an invited audience that includes the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, Edward White, and members of Congress.

One sentence has accompanied this evening for decades. Wilson is said to have declared: “It is like writing history with lightning, and my only regret is that it is all so terribly true.” The American Film Institute catalog repeats it still today, with the caveat of a “reportedly.”

## A source that does not hold up

In a 2010 article, the historian Mark Benbow follows the trail of this sentence, which, as his abstract notes, has appeared in books and articles for about seventy years. One of the historians who cite it, Thomas Cripps, refers in a 1963 article to the New York Post of March 4, 1915. Benbow consults on microfilm the newspaper whose real title is the Evening Post. The sentence is neither in the film's advertisement nor in that day's article, nor in any other issue that month. He does not find it either in the Washington Post or in the Boston Post.

His reasoning goes further: if Griffith had used the line in his promotion, the press would have picked it up, so striking is the image. Wikipedia, for its part, dates to 1937 a popular magazine that attributes the sentence to Wilson, twenty-two years after the screening and thirteen years after the president's death.

## What this establishes, and what it does not

It does not establish that Wilson said nothing. According to Wikipedia, he readily used the lightning metaphor, and he may have said something similar. It establishes only that the source given for the sentence does not contain it, and that Benbow cannot find it in any of the other newspapers he consults.

The file does contain solid evidence, however. The screening did take place, at Dixon's request. The protests against the film were led by the NAACP and others, and the AFI records local bans and cuts through 1931. According to Wikipedia, when these protests reached the White House, Wilson's secretary showed critics a letter saying that the president had been unaware of the nature of the work and had never endorsed it, and that the screening had been a courtesy to an old acquaintance.

The sentence, for its part, makes a single line carry a judgment that these documents do not carry. The screening is documented, the sentence is not, and it is the sentence that has circulated in books and articles. What remains, for anyone who quotes it, is to say where it comes from.

repere.texte: For the sentence “like writing history with lightning,” Thomas Cripps cites in 1963 the New York Post of March 4, 1915. Mark Benbow reads on microfilm the Evening Post, the newspaper's real title: the sentence appears neither on that date nor on any other in the month, nor in the Washington Post, nor in the Boston Post.
repere.source: Benbow, “Birth of a Quotation,” Journal of the Gilded Age and Progressive Era, 2010

carte.punch: The 1915 source of Wilson's sentence about *The Birth of a Nation* remains unfindable.
carte.idee: After the February 18, 1915 screening at the White House, Wilson is credited with a sentence about “history written with lightning.” Mark Benbow looks for its cited source, the New York Post of March 4, 1915: it is not there, nor in the other issues of the month.

quiz.question: What does Mark Benbow's investigation establish about the sentence attributed to Wilson?
choix: That the sentence appears in a March 1915 newspaper, but attributed to Griffith and not to Wilson
That Wilson publicly denied it as early as 1915, through a letter from his secretary
That the source cited for 1915, the New York Post of March 4, does not contain it, nor does any other issue of the month
That Wilson said it to Griffith alone, which explains the absence of a witness
quiz.explication: Benbow reads on microfilm the Evening Post, the real title of the newspaper that Cripps calls the New York Post, and does not find the sentence on any date in March 1915. The letter from Wilson's secretary concerns the endorsement of the work, not the sentence, and nothing in the sources read mentions a single witness or an attribution to Griffith.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who arranged the February 18, 1915 screening at the White House?
choix: Thomas Dixon, who had known Wilson at university
D. W. Griffith, who came to offer the film to the president
Edward White, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is the writer Thomas Dixon, Wilson's university classmate, who requested the screening; Griffith traveled to arrange the details, and White attends only the next day.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to which source does the sentence attributed to Wilson first appear?
choix: A 1963 article signed by the historian Thomas Cripps
The film's advertisement published in March 1915
A popular magazine from 1937, according to Wikipedia
The American Film Institute catalog, published in 1915
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Wikipedia, a popular magazine from 1937 is the first known trace of the sentence, twenty-two years after the screening; Cripps cites it in 1963 although the source he invokes does not contain it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the response from Wilson's circle to the protests against the film, according to Wikipedia?
choix: That Wilson had personally approved the script before shooting
That the president had been unaware of the nature of the work and had never endorsed it
That the screening had never taken place at the White House
That the NAACP had itself requested the screening
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wilson's secretary showed critics a letter stating that the president had been unaware of the nature of the work and had never endorsed it, the screening having been only a courtesy to an old acquaintance.
